title: Shipment Pricing Refactor

title: Patient Vitals Monitor
flaw: useEffect fetching vitals on patientId change has no guard against out-of-order responses, so a stale fetch for a previously selected patient can resolve after a newer one and silently overwrite the currently displayed patient's vitals - an async race condition that only shows up when requests resolve out of order.
key_learnings: useEffect's cleanup runs right before the effect re-runs for a new dependency value (or on unmount) - it's the hook for marking a previous render's in-flight async work as stale.

AbortController only cancels anything if the signal is actually threaded into the request *and* every implementation (real fetch and test fakes) respects it - calling .abort() on a controller nobody passed the signal to is a no-op.
mistakes: First attempt had no cleanup/guard at all, so a stale response could freely overwrite newer state.
Second attempt added an AbortController but never passed abort.signal into fetchVitals, so .abort() had nothing to cancel - same bug persisted.
review_changes: Walked through a local didCancel flag set in the effect's cleanup and checked in .then()/.catch() before calling setState.

Walked through the full AbortController version: extending FetchVitals to accept a signal, threading it into the real fetch(), special-casing AbortError in .catch(), and updating test fakes to honor the signal.
next_focus: Another exercise in the same stale-closure/out-of-order-async-effect family before advancing categories, so it can be mastered before moving on.

title: Watchlist Quote Panel
flaw: useEffect fetching a quote on symbol change has no guard against out-of-order responses, so a stale fetch for a previously selected symbol can resolve after a newer one and silently overwrite the currently displayed symbol's quote - same stale-closure/out-of-order-async-effect race as the prior exercise, held at the same difficulty since that one's status was 'struggled'.
key_learnings: A didCancel-style flag scoped inside the effect's own closure (not a ref) is what flips false in that run's cleanup, so a stale .then()/.catch() belonging to the previous symbol can tell it's no longer current even without AbortController involved.

Threading the AbortController itself into FetchQuote's own signature (rather than constructing one outside and hoping the implementation respects it) is what made cancellation real this time, instead of repeating the prior exercise's abort.signal-never-passed-in mistake.

Keeping a possibly-unstable fetchQuote prop in a ref and leaving it out of the polling effect's dependency array avoids restarting the fetch/poll cycle on every inline-callback re-render, while still using its latest value on the next tick.
mistakes: No functional mistakes in the submitted fix - only a stylistic nit: the `quote.symbol !== symbol` checks in both the hook and the render fallback are redundant once the active-flag/abort guard is in place, since a mismatched quote can never reach state to begin with.
review_changes: Walked through why the prior exercise's AbortController attempt didn't work (signal constructed but never passed into fetchVitals) versus this one, which puts the AbortController in FetchQuote's own signature so any real implementation is forced to receive it.

Walked through the closure-scoped active flag as the mechanism that actually blocks the stale overwrite - cleanup flips it false right before the next effect run, so the earlier symbol's in-flight .then()/.catch() already knows it's stale before it ever checks the abort signal.

Reran the full suite against the original unmodified starter.tsx: both tests this submission added (the out-of-order stale-quote regression and the 2-second auto-refresh poll) fail on the bug and pass on the fix, confirming they actually exercise the race rather than passing vacuously.
next_focus: Category has landed 'completed' - clear to advance the rotation to architecture tradeoffs for the next newly-generated exercise.

Exercises 4-8 (Username Availability Field, Listing Detail Panel, Route Quote Panel, Semester Grades Panel, Fleet Health Panel) are still a pushed-but-unreviewed backlog in this same race-condition family - worth bringing those back for review too as extra reps now that the pattern has clicked.
Next time this pattern shows up, try the plain closure-flag fix directly in the component without reaching for a custom hook/ref abstraction, to keep the minimal version fluent too.

title: Username Availability Field
flaw: Debounced username-availability check has no guard against out-of-order async resolution: the effect keyed on the debounced value calls checkAvailability and sets status/suggestion directly in .then()/.catch() with no comparison against the current debounced value or a request id, so if an earlier keystroke's slower check resolves after a later keystroke's faster one, the stale result silently overwrites the status (and Continue-button enablement) for the username currently in the box - same stale-closure/out-of-order-async-effect race as the prior two exercises, held at the same difficulty and category since the last one (WatchlistQuotePanel) is still unreviewed/assigned and the category hasn't yet landed a 'completed' status since the original 'struggled' entry.

title: Ranked Queue Service
flaw: MatchmakingQueue exposes its internal `players` array as a public, directly-mutable field instead of encapsulating it, so the VIP 'boost to front' admin helper (and any future caller) can unshift players in without going through enqueue's maxSize and duplicate-membership checks - a broken-encapsulation/leaky-abstraction problem where the class can no longer guarantee its own invariants once any external code touches the array directly.
key_learnings: Correctly diagnosed the core fix: make `players` private and turn `boostToFront` into a method, so every mutation is forced through the class's own checks instead of being reachable from outside.

Split enqueue's size/duplicate checks into their own reusable methods so boostToFront (and future methods) could call into the same checks - good instinct for avoiding a second copy of the invariant logic.

For an already-queued player, chose splice-out-then-unshift over a swap-with-front-element specifically to preserve the relative order of every other player in the queue - correctly reasoned that a swap would disturb two players' positions instead of one, which matters for a matchmaking queue's fairness/ordering semantics.

Party Queue: checked capacity for the whole group before enqueueing any of them, so the group is added atomically and always ends up adjacent; added an optional partyId for future group-aware dequeue logic.
Discussed via chat rather than submitted as code for this session - approach was described and reasoned through verbally, not verified against the exercise's own test suite.
mistakes: Applied the same 'is there space' size check to both branches of boostToFront: the brand-new-player branch (where it's correct, since that's a net +1 on the queue) and the already-queued-player branch (where it's wrong, since splice-then-unshift is net +0 - moving someone already counted in the queue doesn't need any additional space). As written, boosting a player who's already in a full queue - the single most common time someone would actually want this - would be incorrectly rejected, even though it can never violate the max-size invariant.
review_changes: Walked through why gating both branches behind the same size check is a boundary-condition bug: the check only protects the case where the queue's total count actually grows, not the case where an existing member is just being repositioned.

Discussed splice+unshift vs. swap-with-front-element as two ways to move an existing player to the front, and confirmed splice+unshift is the better call for preserving the rest of the queue's relative order - swap would silently reorder a second, uninvolved player too.
next_focus: When a shared guard gets reused across multiple branches during a refactor, check whether the guard's condition is actually true for each branch individually (net change to the invariant it protects), rather than copying it because the mutation 'feels' similarly risky.

This session's review was conversational (no code pushed/tested) - worth doing a from-scratch coded pass on a similar encapsulation-smell exercise at some point to confirm the fix holds up against the actual test suite, not just verbal description.

title: Payroll Event Processor
flaw: PayrollEvent models four mutually-exclusive event shapes as one flat interface with a `type` discriminator plus a pile of unrelated optional fields, instead of a discriminated union - so an event object can carry fields that don't belong to its type (or omit required ones) with no compile error, and toLineItem's final branch is an unconditional catch-all ('correction - and, for now, anything else') with no exhaustiveness check, so a new event type added later silently falls into the correction branch (wrong description, wrong amount) instead of failing to compile. Regenerated to replace an earlier (incorrectly generated) debugging exercise - see exercise 5's note. First appearance of the typescript-modeling category.
key_learnings: Discriminated union (base type intersected with a per-type variant) + a switch over the tag + assertNever(event) in default is the right shape - it closes both problems the README called out: invalid field combinations become unconstructable, and a forgotten branch for a new event type becomes a compile error instead of a silent default-branch fallthrough.

assertNever only forces a compile error for code the compiler actually type-checks. Adding the 'rehire' bonus type and a matching handler proved the mechanism works, but that guarantee doesn't automatically extend across any boundary the compiler doesn't see, like a hand-constructed test object, JSON.parse output, or an `as` cast.

A field marked 'required' on a union member but still backed by a `?? 0`/`?? 'Bonus'` runtime fallback isn't really required - the fallback is standing in for exactly the undefined case the required annotation was supposed to rule out.

Partial<T> over a union type only exposes the keys common to every branch (keyof of a union is the intersection of each member's keys, not the union of them), so a test seam helper typed as `Partial<PayrollEvent>` silently lost access to every type-specific field the moment the type became a discriminated union, rather than erroring loudly.

vitest (via esbuild) does not type-check test files, so a broken seam helper's test suite can pass 8/8 at the same time `tsc --noEmit` fails on the same files - confirmed directly by running both against identical code and getting opposite verdicts.
mistakes: Made every PayrollEvent field required per-branch but left the `?? 0`/`?? 'Bonus'` fallbacks in the handler functions in place 'just to pass tests,' which meant the new required-field guarantee didn't actually hold against the test file itself.

Added the `rehire` branch, its handler, and the matching switch case correctly, but didn't update the test file's seam helpers (`hireEvent`, `terminationEvent`, etc.) to match the new discriminated-union shape - they were still typed as `overrides: Partial<PayrollEvent>`, which no longer type-checked once PayrollEvent became a union, so `tsc --noEmit` failed even though `npm test` passed. Needed a second push to fix, after the first claimed fix didn't actually change the file.
Left an unused `import { assert } from "vitest"` in starter.ts; flagged but left unfixed by choice to move on.
review_changes: Confirmed the discriminated-union/assertNever/helper-extraction approach is correct and matches both goals stated in the exercise's README.

Walked through why keeping required fields alongside `?? 0` fallbacks doesn't close the gap the exercise is about, tying it to the general principle that compile-time guarantees only hold for code the compiler actually runs over, not data crossing an unchecked boundary.

Verified the bonus challenge directly: added the `rehire` type/handler/case on the `payrolleventprocessor` branch, ran `tsc --noEmit`, and confirmed assertNever's exhaustiveness check genuinely works - no error once rehire was handled.

Found and diagnosed the Partial<PayrollEvent>-over-a-union bug in the seam helpers by actually running `tsc --noEmit` against the pushed branch rather than taking the description at face value - it failed with 5 real errors while `npm test` passed cleanly, demonstrating the vitest-doesn't-type-check point concretely.
After the fix was pushed, re-ran `tsc --noEmit` and `npm test` again and confirmed the seam-helper errors were gone (8/8 tests still passing), leaving only the pre-existing unused-import nit.
next_focus: Remove the unused `assert` import from starter.ts - flagged, left open by choice.

When a type becomes a discriminated union, check any existing `Partial<T>` usages elsewhere in the codebase (test helpers, mock builders, etc.) - keyof a union only covers fields common to every branch, so Partial<Union> silently weakens instead of erroring, which is easy to miss.

Treat 'field is required, but a runtime fallback is still there to handle it being missing' as a smell worth catching early in future typescript-modeling exercises - if removing the fallback would break a test, the field isn't actually required yet.

title: Product Grid Search
flaw: ProductGrid passes a brand-new inline arrow function as ProductCard's onAddToCart prop on every render, which defeats ProductCard's React.memo wrapper - so every visible card re-renders on each keystroke in the unrelated search input, even though each card's own product data hasn't changed; at full catalog scale this is a real rendering-performance cost on every character typed. Regenerated to replace an earlier (incorrectly generated) debugging exercise - see exercise 5's note. First appearance of the react-state-performance category.
key_learnings: memo only pays off if every single prop handed to the wrapped component is reference-stable across renders - one unstable prop (even a function the component never reads any closed-over value from) is enough to defeat the shallow-compare bailout and force a re-render regardless of whether the 'important' props changed.

The inline wrapper `(id) => onAddToCart(id)` was functionally a no-op - same signature, same call, no transformation - so the correct fix was deleting it and passing `onAddToCart` straight through, not wrapping it in useCallback (there was nothing to memoize, since nothing was being captured or transformed).

useMemo memoizes a computation inside the component that owns it; it does nothing to stabilize a value being handed down as a prop to a memoized child unless that value IS the memoized result itself. Wrapping the filter in useMemo and stabilizing the callback passed to ProductCard are two unrelated jobs.

Correctly avoided reaching for a debounce despite considering it, which would have violated the README's explicit restriction against delaying/removing live-as-you-type filtering - recognized the uncertainty and asked rather than guessing at an approach that was off-limits anyway.
mistakes: First pass added `useMemo` around the filter with `search` in its own dependency array, which still recomputes on every keystroke (the thing it was meant to prevent) and does nothing about prop stability on the actual memoized child - left the real bug (the inline arrow passed as onAddToCart) completely untouched, so the reported slowdown was unchanged by this attempt.

Initially reported the inline-arrow fix as pushed when the branch still had the unmodified wrapper - needed a second push before `onAddToCart={(id) => onAddToCart(id)}` was actually replaced with `onAddToCart={onAddToCart}`.
review_changes: Walked through why `useMemo` with `search` in its deps doesn't save any work in this exact scenario (the input that changes on every keystroke is also the thing gating the memo), versus when useMemo would actually help (a parent re-rendering for unrelated reasons while its own inputs stay the same).

Identified that the inline arrow wrapping onAddToCart had no logic of its own - compared its signature to onAddToCart's directly to show it could just be deleted rather than replaced with useCallback.

Verified the fix with the official test suite (5/5 passing) plus `tsc --noEmit` (clean), then wrote an ad hoc render-count probe test (not part of the official suite, which doesn't check render counts) confirming memo actually bails out now: changing the search text to drop one card left the other two cards' render counts unchanged instead of ticking up.
next_focus: When `memo` isn't preventing re-renders, check every prop passed to the wrapped component for reference stability individually, rather than assuming the fix is about memoizing more computation upstream.

Before reaching for `useCallback`/`useMemo`, check whether the value even needs wrapping - an inline function with no captured transformation can often just be deleted in favor of passing the original reference directly.
Push and re-check before reporting a fix as done - this session twice had a described fix not actually present on the pushed branch yet.

title: Lineup Eligibility Rules
flaw: canAddToLineup and canCompleteTrade independently re-implement the same player-eligibility rule rather than sharing one source of truth, and the two copies have already drifted: canAddToLineup blocks injured_reserve players from any slot except ir_slot, but canCompleteTrade never grew that check (its comment says IR players historically couldn't be traded at all), so a trade can currently place an injured_reserve player directly into a starter slot - a duplicated-business-rule-gone-stale smell rather than a crash. Regenerated to replace an earlier (incorrectly generated) debugging exercise - see exercise 5's note. Second appearance of code-review (exercise 1 was first, diff 1, still unreviewed), held at difficulty 2.
key_learnings: Correctly diagnosed and fixed the actual drift: extracted a single shared `handleSlotRestriction(player, slot)` helper and routed both `canAddToLineup` and `canCompleteTrade` through it, so the suspended/injured_reserve checks live in exactly one place and the two surfaces can no longer disagree about the same player/slot combination - matches the exercise's explicit goal.

Passing `destinationSlot` straight through to the shared helper rather than ignoring it meant the extraction didn't reintroduce an unused-parameter situation, even with the exercise's tsconfig already relaxed for that case.
mistakes: Left the pre-existing test 'currently allows trading an injured_reserve player straight into a starter slot' (which asserts `toBe(true)`) completely unchanged, even though the fix's entire purpose is to make that `false` now. Running the suite against the submitted fix shows 7/8 passing with exactly that one failure - a real regression against the test file as it stands, not a flaw in the production logic.
Declined to update that test when flagged, so the exercise is being logged with correct production code sitting behind a red test suite.
review_changes: Verified the fix with `tsc --noEmit` (clean) and the full test suite (7/8 passing), confirming the single failure is the pre-existing bug-documenting test rather than a new regression introduced by the refactor.

Explained why that specific test needs to change despite the README's 'maintain the spirit of the original test' restriction: that test's entire spirit was 'this is the current, not-yet-fixed bug,' and the fix's job is specifically to invalidate it - keeping its assertion frozen just pins the regression back in.
next_focus: Go back and flip that one test to `expect(...).toBe(false)` (and rename it away from 'currently allows...') so the suite is actually green - the only remaining step to close this exercise out cleanly.

When a fix is explicitly meant to change observable behavior rather than just internal structure, check for any test that documents the OLD behavior as current/expected - 'maintain the spirit of the original test' doesn't apply when a test's whole spirit was 'this is the bug to be fixed.'

title: Now Playing Crossfade
flaw: NowPlayingBar's track-change effect calls crossfade(...) but discards its returned cancel function instead of returning/storing it, so the interval crossfade starts is never cleared when the index changes again before that fade finishes - skipping again mid-fade leaves the previous interval running in the background, still calling setVolume against a track that's no longer current and overlapping with the new fade's calls. A missing-effect-cleanup/orphaned-interval bug, deliberately a different debugging sub-skill from exercises 2-4's async-fetch-ordering race family, now that that family landed 'completed' on exercise 3. Difficulty raised to 3 (third appearance of debugging, after struggled@2 then completed@2) and domain changed to avoid repeating the race-condition pattern yet again. Regenerated to replace an earlier (incorrectly generated) debugging exercise that was the 8th race-condition repeat in a row - see exercise 5's note.

title: Fare Upgrade Engine
flaw: evaluateUpgrade conflates checking upgrade eligibility with committing it: the same function that answers 'can this passenger upgrade' also mutates flight.seatsAvailable and the passenger's fare class/step count as a side effect, so there is no way to safely preview eligibility (e.g. for a 'See if I qualify' UI) without also consuming a seat - a query/command-separation violation that only becomes a real problem once eligibility needs to be checkable more than once without consequence.
